key: He shall not make himself unclean for his father, or for his mother, for his brother, or for his sister, when they die; because his consecration unto God is upon his head.
s: After wine and the razor, the Nazirite law turns to the dead; Ibn Ezra, on 6:7, takes as not far-fetched the view deriving the Nazirite’s name from the crown on his head, and calls whoever is free of the world’s desires the true king, crowned.
src: Ibn Ezra, Commentary on the Torah, on Numbers 6:7, Hebrew (Sefaria’s “On Your Way”), Sefaria export 3f10136 (2026)

opened.edition: Ibn Ezra on Numbers, Hebrew “On Your Way”, Sefaria export 3f10136

evidence.words: ויש אומרים כי מלת נזיר מגזרת נזר והעד כי נזר אלהיו על ראשו ואיננו רחוק ודע כי כל בני אדם עבדי תאות העולם והמלך באמת שיש לו נזר ועטרת מלכות בראשו כל מי שהוא חפשי מן התאות
evidence.gloss: Some say that the word nazir comes from nezer (crown), the proof being ‘the nezer of his God is upon his head’, and this is not far-fetched. Know that all human beings are slaves to the desires of the world, and the king in truth, who has a crown (nezer) and a royal diadem on his head, is whoever is free of the desires.

reason: The problem holds: after ‘those who derive…’ the absolute clause ‘the true king being…’ could be read as part of the reported view rather than as Ibn Ezra’s own remark. Re-opened packet.js tanakh 44 --verse 6:7: the derivation from nezer is reported (ויש אומרים) and judged not far-fetched (ואיננו רחוק); the true-king remark is his own (ודע), and it ties back to the crown, since his true king is the one with a nezer and royal diadem on his head. The sentence now gives the remark to him with his own verb and keeps the crown (‘the true king, crowned’, his נזר ועטרת מלכות בראשו); ‘the world’s desires’ is his תאות העולם.
